title: Acasta Gneiss: Earth's oldest intact rock

facts.text: Zircons in the Acasta Gneiss Complex of Canada's Northwest Territories crystallized about 4.03 Ga; as of 2026 these beds are Earth's oldest known felsic crust.
The ICS starts the Archean at 4,031 ± 3 Ma, the age of the oldest known intact rock formations.
The gneiss belongs to the Slave Craton and records more than a billion years of magmatism and metamorphism, from over 4.0 to 2.9 Ga.
Tonalites from about 4.0 Ga are among the first larger pieces of continental crust, built of light rock that rose during partial melting.
Its 3.94 Ga tonalitic gneisses partly derive from 4.2 Ga granite magma, showing that crust was already being reworked in the Eoarchean.

title: Carbon cycle takes its basic form

facts.text: Early carbon isotope ratios closely match today's, suggesting the carbon cycle's fundamental features were established as early as about 4 Ga.
Much of the carbon dioxide in the young atmosphere dissolved in water and reacted with calcium and magnesium from weathered rock, building carbonate sediments.
Plate tectonics keeps rearranging the continents, which moves carbon dioxide to and from large continental carbonate stores.
In the carbon cycle, carbon is stored for very long periods as limestone or fossil fuels.

title: DNA replaces RNA as genetic material

facts.text: Early life probably used RNA as its genetic material; DNA evolved later as a more chemically stable store of genetic information.
Virologist Luis Villarreal proposes that viruses carried RNA genes into DNA genomes during this transition, around 4 Ga, before the last universal common ancestor.
LUCA most likely already had DNA; the exact timeline and mechanism of the switch remain open questions.

contested_note: The c. 4 Ga date rests on one virologist's proposal, and the timeline of DNA's origin is still an open question.

facts.text: Mountain building raised the Napier range of East Antarctica, dated to 4000 ± 200 Ma.
Its faulting and folding may have produced some of Earth's first metamorphic rocks.
Metamorphism most commonly happens deep in the crust, where buried rocks undergo intense changes in temperature and pressure during mountain building.

title: End of the Late Heavy Bombardment

facts.text: The final phase of the Late Heavy Bombardment is placed at about 3,920–3,850 Ma; impacts stayed frequent in the early Archean.
Tungsten isotopes suggest most gold in the crust came from the mantle after a meteorite bombardment about 3.9 billion years ago.
Lunar impact-melt ages cluster near 3.9 Ga, but critics and impact models favour several smaller bombardment episodes over one cataclysm.

title: Possible earliest life at Akilia, Greenland

facts.text: Graphite in metamorphosed rock on Akilia Island, southwest Greenland, is low in carbon-13, which may mark organic matter from living things.
An igneous band cutting the rock shows it is no younger than 3.85 billion years; 3,850 Ma Greenland apatite is likewise enriched in carbon-12.
The rocks' sedimentary origin, age and carbon have all been questioned, and the find sparked debate over photosynthetic life before 3.8 Ga.

contested_note: Whether the Akilia rocks are sedimentary, how old they are and whether their carbon is biological are all disputed.

title: East European Craton begins to form

facts.text: The first rocks of the Ukrainian Shield and Voronezh Massif were laid down, starting the East European Craton.
This Archean crust, 3.2–3.8 Ga old, lies in the craton's southwest and east.
Its Sarmatian part holds Archean terranes of about 3.7–2.7 Ga.
The first complete continental masses, or cratons, built of granite blocks, appeared on Earth around 3,800 Ma.
Cratons are old, stable parts of continental lithosphere with deep roots; most formed in the Archean.
Felsic magmas rose on the eastern edge of the Antarctic craton as the first great continental mass began to gather.
Antarctic zircons of 3.9–3.0 Ga suggest recycling within the crust was key to building the first cratons.
About 39% of modern continental crust formed in the Archean.
The oldest known banded iron formations, at Isua in Greenland's greenstone belt, date from about 3,800–3,700 Ma.
Iron isotopes in them point to extremely low oxygen and to iron oxidized by anoxygenic photosynthesis.
Algoma-type iron formations formed mainly in the Archean; deposition later peaked near the eon's end.
Volcanic and sedimentary sequences about 3,800 and 3,700 Ma old built the Isua belt, the largest exposure of Eoarchean supracrustal rock on Earth.
Isua pillow basalt, formed in an underwater eruption, shows that liquid water existed 3.8 billion years ago.
Whether the belt formed by plate tectonics or by heat-pipe or plume volcanism is contentious, part of the wider debate on early tectonics.

title: Yangtze Block of South China forms

facts.text: The Yangtze Block, the northwestern part of the South China Craton, is thought to have formed around 3.8–3.2 Ga.
3.8 Ga detrital zircons preserve remnants of this ancient crust.
Its Kongling Complex holds China's oldest rocks, with zircon ages of 3.3–2.9 Ga.

facts.text: Western Australia's Pilbara Craton holds crust up to 3.8 billion years old, intruded by granite domes and greenstone belts of about 3.5–3.2 Ga.
With the Kaapvaal Craton it is one of only two pristine Archean crusts left on Earth.
Detrital zircons of 3.8–3.6 Ga show crust was already eroding 300 million years before its oldest surviving rocks.
The craton stabilized around 3,600 Ma, as continents possibly gathered into Vaalbara.
By 2.97 Ga the West Pilbara Terrane had collided with and joined the East Pilbara Terrane.

facts.text: Anaerobic microbes, including chemotrophs and photosynthesisers, appear from about 3.7 Ga.
This simpler photosynthesis arose not long after life began and released no oxygen, using donors such as hydrogen sulfide, sulfur or iron instead of water.
Bacteria using it made ATP from a proton gradient, a mechanism used by nearly all later organisms.
Geochemical evidence suggests it emerged 3.3–3.5 Ga; fossils thought to be filamentous photosynthesisers date to 3.4 Ga.
The first photosynthesisers may have arisen at acidic hydrothermal vents, using their faint geothermal light and hydrogen sulfide rather than water.

title: Earliest evidence of Earth's magnetic field

facts.text: Evidence from Greenland, published in 2024, shows Earth had a magnetic field by 3,700 million years ago.
Earlier paleomagnetic work on Australian lava and South African conglomerate showed a field since at least about 3,450 Ma.
Earth, like most planets, makes its field through the motion of electrically conducting fluids.
By 3.5 Ga the field, driven by currents in the molten outer core, helped stop the solar wind stripping away the atmosphere.

title: Earliest traces of life at Isua

facts.text: About 3.7 Ga metasedimentary rocks at Isua, Greenland, hold graphite whose carbon isotopes suggest biological fractionation.
It is the earliest evidence of life from a rock unit rather than a single mineral grain.
In 2016 a team reported dome-shaped stromatolites 1–4 cm high, 220 million years older than those of the Dresser Formation.
The layers sit on volcanic rock dated 3.709 Ga and beneath beds dated 3.695 Ga.
The stromatolites are disputed: a 2018 study, joined by one original proponent, put the shapes down to rock deformation.

facts.text: South Africa's Kaapvaal Craton formed and stabilised between 3.7 and 2.6 Ga as large granite batholiths thickened its crust.
Its oldest parts are tonalitic gneisses of about 3.6–3.7 Ga, joined by granite-greenstone terranes of 3.0–3.5 Ga.
With the Pilbara Craton it is one of only two pristine Archean crusts known.
Its granite is exposed in the core of the Vredefort impact structure.
From 3.0 to 2.7 Ga, continent–arc collision built basins filled with thick volcanic and sedimentary sequences.

facts.text: The Wyoming Craton began as a 100,000 km² Archean craton with gneisses of 3.6–3.0 Ga.
Late Archean magmatism and plate movements modified it, and by the end of the eon its three subprovinces had joined.
Its rocks reach 3.5 Ga, with detrital zircons up to 4.0 Ga.

title: Vaalbara supercontinent

facts.text: The Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons may have joined as Vaalbara, one of Earth's earliest supercontinents, as far back as about 3.6 Ga.
The two cratons show strikingly similar rock sequences from 3.5 to 2.7 Ga, and share 3.5–3.2 Ga impact spherule layers.
Paleomagnetic data hint they were linked even at 3.87 Ga, but a Paleoarchean proto-Vaalbara cannot be proven.
By 2.78–2.77 Ga the cratons lay 30° of latitude apart, so Vaalbara had broken up by about 2.8 Ga, though these reconstructions are ambiguous.
Some scientists dispute Vaalbara, explaining the shared features as global processes, or date its assembly to the Mesoarchean or Neoarchean.

contested_note: Whether and when Vaalbara existed is debated, and it competes with the largely incompatible Ur hypothesis.

facts.text: India's Dharwar Craton, the oldest part of the Indian peninsula, formed between 3.6 and 2.5 Ga.
Its three blocks joined between 2560 and 2500 Ma, closing all of its subduction zones.
Around 3350 Ma, ridge push drove oceanic crust down into the mantle, and slab melting produced its TTG crust.

facts.text: Lavas and sediments of the Barberton belt in South Africa and Eswatini were laid down between 3.5 and 3.2 Ga.
The area grew in two episodes of terrane accretion, about 3.5 and 3.2 Ga, matching pulses of TTG magmatism.
Its Makhonjwa Mountains are among the oldest in Africa, and its rocks hold some of the oldest traces of life.

facts.text: Eight spherule layers (S1–S8) in the Barberton belt, about 3.5–3.2 Ga, record at least four and perhaps eight or more impacts.
Spherules of 3.5 Ga in South Africa and Western Australia are the oldest known products of impacts on Earth.
A 2024 review counts 36 layers from 3.47–3.22 Ga and 2.63–2.49 Ga, a 'tail' of the Late Heavy Bombardment.
The record from 3.2 Ga includes impacts by objects up to 100 km wide.

facts.text: Stromatolites in the Dresser Formation of the Pilbara Craton, deposited about 3483–3479 Ma, are the earliest direct evidence of life.
Microbially induced sedimentary structures of the same age record microbial mats, the earliest life with good fossil evidence.
Its North Pole chert also holds microfossils, mat fabrics and carbon and sulfur biosignatures that suggest heat-loving microbes.
The stromatolites grew mostly in a shallow lagoon or flooded caldera where seawater mixed with hydrothermal fluids; some formed near hot springs on land.
The earliest undisputed evidence of life dates from at least 3.5 Ga, from the stromatolite record.

facts.text: By about 3.4 Ga nitrogen was the main gas of a then-stable second atmosphere, which also held methane, carbon dioxide, water vapor and sulfur gases.
Volcanic outgassing, supplemented by gases from huge asteroids of the Late Heavy Bombardment, produced this Archean atmosphere.
It was anoxic and weakly reducing: oxygen stayed around or below 0.001% of today's level until about 2.4 Ga.
Sulfur-isotope signals rule out significant oxygen before about 2.45 Ga; river and delta grains of pyrite, siderite and uraninite older than 2.4 Ga also point to anoxia.
Any oxygen made by early photosynthesis was quickly used up oxidizing ferrous iron, sulfur and methane at the surface.
Trondhjemitic and tonalitic granitic rocks intruded mafic–ultramafic greenstone in the central Kaapvaal Craton, forming South Africa's Johannesburg Dome.
U–Pb dating of single zircons gives 3340 ± 3 Ma, the oldest granitoid phase recognised there so far.
Later mafic dykes and granodiorites, some dated 3121 ± 5 Ma, support the view that the craton grew episodically by accretion.
The Zimbabwe Craton's Tokwe and Rhodesdale segments, with rocks as old as 3.46 Ga, stabilized about 3.3 Ga.
The craton formed by the suture of these two smaller crustal blocks.
With the Kaapvaal Craton and Limpopo Belt it rests on a buoyant mantle root about 250 km thick that yields diamonds.

facts.text: South Africa's Fig Tree Formation, about 3.28–3.22 Ga, holds stromatolites and fossils of microscopic life about 3.26 billion years old.

facts.text: An asteroid about 37–58 km wide hit Earth around 3.26 Ga, leaving the S2 spherule layer in the Barberton Greenstone Belt.
Its crater may have been almost 480 km across, two and a half times the diameter of Chicxulub's.
It probably shook the whole planet with strong earthquakes and raised megatsunamis thousands of metres high.
It boiled the ocean surface, evaporating tens of metres of the global ocean.
The Moodies Group, laid down about 3.22 Ga in South Africa and Eswatini, holds Earth's oldest well-preserved siliciclastic tidal deposits.
Microbial mats flourished on its tidal flats, and its microfossils are among the few accepted Archean examples.
It overlies the Fig Tree Formation in the Barberton Greenstone Belt of the Kaapvaal craton.

title: Oxygenic photosynthesis evolves

facts.text: Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesisers appears about 3.2 Ga, with local free oxygen around carbonate-platform stromatolites.
Cyanobacteria arose in fresh water or on land in the middle Archean; claims reach back to 3.5 Ga, and 2026 genetic work considers a 2.9–3 Ga origin established.
Cyanobacteria split water and released oxygen as waste, which first oxidized dissolved iron in the oceans to form iron ore.
Oxygen built up only slowly, poisoning many bacteria and eventually triggering the Great Oxygenation Event after the Archean.
Pilbara biomarkers of 2.7 Ga, once read as cyanobacteria and eukaryote steranes, were later shown to be contamination.

contested_note: The timing of oxygenic photosynthesis is debated, with claims from 3.5 Ga down to certain evidence by 2.4 Ga.

title: Hot Mesoarchean climate under a methane greenhouse

facts.text: Oxygen isotopes in Mesoarchean cherts suggest ocean temperatures of about 55–85 °C, though weathering studies suggest averages below 50 °C.
High levels of methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere may explain the warmth; the climate was at least temperate.
Volcanoes supplied the carbon dioxide and early microbes the methane, which lasted longer in an atmosphere without oxygen.
Nitrogen levels were probably similar to today's, so nitrogen played little part in warming the planet.
Methane broken apart by sunlight may also have made an organic haze, which would have had a cooling, anti-greenhouse effect.

title: Ur supercontinent forms

facts.text: Ur is a hypothetical supercontinent of rocks now in India, western Australia and southern Africa, formed around 3.1 Ga.
Its assembly is put at 3,200–2,600 Ma, covering 12–16% of today's continental crust.
The main argument is that cratons stable by about 3 Ga all sat in one region of Pangaea.
Rogers proposed Ur later grew into East Gondwana by accreting to East Antarctica.
A conflicting hypothesis joins western Australia and southern Africa as Vaalbara; most proposed Archean supercontinents are controversial.

contested_note: Ur is hypothetical and controversial, and its reconstruction is largely incompatible with the rival Vaalbara hypothesis.

facts.text: The Saamian orogeny built an extensive area of tonalitic-trondhjemitic crust in Fennoscandia between 3.1 and 2.9 Ga.

title: Miralga (North Pole Dome) impact structure

facts.text: Shatter cones near Marble Bar in the Pilbara reveal the Miralga, or North Pole Dome, impact structure; its crater may have exceeded 100 km.
A March 2025 study dated it to 3,470 ± 2 Ma, which would make it the oldest known impact structure by over a billion years.
A July 2025 study found shatter cones in rocks younger than 2.71 Ga, so the impact came after then and before 400 Ma.
A 2026 study dated impact-recrystallized zircon to 3.024 Ga and hydrothermal apatite to 3.019 Ga.
Spherules in its Antarctic Creek Member record a 3.5 Ga impact, but such spherules can travel far from their crater.

contested_note: Its age is disputed: 3.47 Ga (March 2025), between 2.71 Ga and 400 Ma (July 2025), or about 3.02 Ga (2026).

title: Possible onset of modern plate tectonics

facts.text: A possible onset of plate tectonics is placed around 3 Ga, but its timing is still debated.
The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction, including an oceanic arc at a Pilbara convergent margin about 3.12 Ga.
Minerals in ancient diamonds suggest the supercontinent cycle began roughly 3 Ga; diamonds from crustal eclogite became common after 3.0 Ga.
A hotter Paleoarchean mantle ruled out modern plate tectonics; some suggest a stagnant lid instead.
Other estimates range from the Hadean, over 4 Ga, to 2.2 Ga, or 800 Ma for fully modern-style tectonics.

facts.text: Continental crust grew relatively fast on the shields between 3.0 and 2.5 Ga, with widespread mantle melting and crustal growth in the Neoarchean.
Before 3.7 Ga continents held under 10% of today's crust, and there is little evidence of continental crust before 3.5 Ga.
Roughly 20–25% of today's continental crust existed by 3.0 Ga; after rapid crustal evolution it reached about 60% by 2.6 Ga.
The remaining fifth of the continental crust formed only during the last 2.5 billion years.
TTG rocks, major components of Archean cratons, formed by partial melting of water-rich mafic rock at high pressure; whether subduction drove this is debated.

title: Pongola glaciation, Earth's oldest known glaciation

facts.text: The Pongola glaciation, from about 2.985 to 2.837 Ga, is the oldest known glaciation on Earth.
Its traces are diamictites of the Pongola Supergroup's Mozaan Formation in KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini.
It interrupted a Mesoarchean climate that was warm or temperate, kept mild by high methane and carbon dioxide.
Ice reached a palaeolatitude of 48 degrees; whether it extended toward the tropics is uncertain.
Sulfur-isotope changes suggest it may be tied to an early, short-lived oxygenation of the atmosphere.

facts.text: A transient episode of higher oxygen occurred around 2,980–2,960 Ma, in an atmosphere that otherwise had almost no free oxygen.
Oases of relatively high oxygen existed in some nearshore shallow seas by the Mesoarchean.
Sulfur isotopes link the coeval Pongola glaciation to an early, short-lived oxygenation.

title: Witwatersrand Basin fills with gold-bearing sediments

facts.text: From about 2.97 to 2.71 Ga, rivers and a sea laid 5–7 km of mostly sedimentary rock in the Witwatersrand Basin on the Kaapvaal craton.
As uplift pushed the sea back, braided river deltas on a wide coastal plain concentrated heavy minerals: gold, pyrite and uraninite.
The basin holds the world's largest known gold reserves: over 40,000 tonnes mined, about 22% of all gold above ground.

conflicts.note: Transvaal Supergroup: single age for the underlying Witwatersrand Basin

facts.text: The North Atlantic Craton, now in West Greenland, Labrador and northwest Scotland, grew as terranes collided in a series of orogenies.
The Akia, Isukasia and Kapisilik terranes collided about 2950 Ma; more terranes merged 2850–2700 Ma and around Nuuk 2650–2580 Ma.
Regional magmatism, tectonism and metamorphism reworked and stabilized the craton in the Mesoarchean to Neoarchean.
Western Australia's Yilgarn Craton was assembled between about 2.94 and 2.63 Ga from many terranes of older crust, mostly formed 3.2–2.8 Ga.
Its bedrock includes the Narryer Gneiss, home of the Jack Hills zircons, under greenstone belts of about 2.70–2.55 Ga.
Most of its gold was deposited 2650–2630 Ma, after an earlier gold event at 2660–2655 Ma during crustal extension.
The Abitibi greenstone belt of Ontario and Quebec, one of the world's largest Archean greenstone belts, formed 2,800–2,600 Ma.
Mostly volcanic, it is a stack of thrusted subterranes like those of paired arc–back-arc systems, with intrusions of 2,675–2,700 Ma throughout.
It contains the huge 2,707–2,696 Ma Blake River Megacaldera Complex.

title: Limpopo Belt joins the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe cratons

facts.text: Late Archean metamorphism welded the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe cratons along the 250 km wide Limpopo Belt about 2.8–2.5 Ga.
High-grade metamorphism in the belt ceased once the two cratons were stabilized together.
High-pressure granulites formed in the belt about 2.69 Ga.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth: formation of the Limpopo Belt

facts.text: Neoarchean crust, 85% of the North China Craton's basement, formed in two pulses, 2.8–2.7 and 2.6–2.5 Ga.
Whether its blocks amalgamated about 2.5 Ga (Kusky's model) or only at 1.85 Ga (Zhao's model) is debated.
Banded iron formations and schists were laid down there after the Fupingian orogeny of 2550 Ma.
A thick pile of sedimentary and volcanic rock filled the Fortescue, Hamersley and Turee Creek basins on the Pilbara from about 2.78 to 2.42 Ga.
U–Pb dating puts the base of the Mount Bruce Supergroup at 2768 ± 16 Ma.
The Hamersley Basin on the Pilbara's southern margin was the last stable marine and river setting between the Yilgarn and Pilbara before rifting.

facts.text: The Slave Craton's main stabilization came about 2.75 Ga, marked by abundant peridotite in its mantle root.
Kaapvaal shows a similar growth peak, suggesting much of Earth's continental lithospheric mantle formed in the Neoarchean.
Diamonds from craton roots are often over 3 billion years old; the Slave's oldest, 3.5–3.3 Ga, imply an early thick root.

facts.text: Western Australia's Tumbiana Formation, about 2727–2715 Ma, was laid down in the oldest known carbonate-rich lake system.
Its limestones hold stromatolites such as Alcheringa narrina and organic-walled microfossils, adding to the few accepted Archean microfossils.
The microfossils' size and protrusions resemble eukaryotic microbes, but such features are not unique to eukaryotes and their affinity remains obscure.

verification.title: Organic-walled microfossils from the ca. 2.7 Ga Tumbiana Formation of Western Australia

title: Kenorland supercontinent forms

facts.text: Kenorland, a hypothetical supercontinent, formed about 2.72 Ga through the accretion of Neoarchean cratons and new continental crust.
Its core, the Baltic or Fennoscandian Shield, traces back over 3.1 Ga, and Arctica formed part of it.
It broke up sometime after 2.45–2.1 Ga into proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn and Kalahari.
Alternatively the cratons formed separate supercratons, Superia and Sclavia; the Slave collided with Sclavia by 2.6 Ga, and Superia's final assembly came at 2520 Ma.
Kenorland's final assembly was finished by 2,600–2,550 Ma, with the Superior and Wyoming provinces side by side.

contested_note: Kenorland is hypothetical; the cratons may instead have gathered into separate supercratons such as Superia and Sclavia.

title: Ventersdorp lavas flood the Kaapvaal craton

facts.text: Massive outpourings of lava, the Ventersdorp lavas, erupted about 2.715 Ga and abruptly ended deposition of the Witwatersrand's gold-rich Central Rand Group.
Their cause is speculative: one source links them to the Kaapvaal craton's collision with the Zimbabwe Craton, another places them in a phase of rifting.
The lavas and the overlying Transvaal Supergroup were later warped into rings by the Vredefort impact.
The Blake River Megacaldera Complex of Ontario and Quebec, the first known Precambrian supervolcano, began forming about 2,707 Ma.
Its first caldera, Misema, is 80 km long and 40 km wide, built from at least two coalescing mafic shield volcanoes.
Later phases built the New Senator Caldera (2704–2701 Ma) and the Noranda Caldera (2696 Ma), with 7–9 km of erupted rock.

title: Global komatiite eruption and possible mantle overturn

facts.text: A major eruption of komatiite lava, possibly global, occurred around 2,705 Ma and may mark an overturn of the mantle.
Komatiite magma forms when 30–40% of mantle rock melts at very high pressure, leaving a residue like Archean lithospheric mantle.
Komatiite lavas, erupting at up to about 1600 °C, formed almost only in the Archean, when the mantle may have been 100–250 °C hotter.
Another pulse of oxygenation came about 2,700 Ma; some consider it a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event.
Skewed sulfur isotopes in pyrites show a small rise in atmospheric oxygen around this time.
Cyanobacteria had appeared by at least 2.7 Ga, and an oxygen-containing atmosphere began to develop in the late Archean.
Most scholars still place the start of the Great Oxygenation Event in the Paleoproterozoic, about 2,400 Ma.

facts.text: The Stillwater complex, a large layered mafic intrusion in southern Montana, was intruded into older gneisses about 2.7 Ga.
About 5,500 m of its layers are exposed along 48 km of the Beartooth Mountains.
It holds large reserves of chromium and platinum-group metals such as palladium, and resembles South Africa's Bushveld complex.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth seed, uncited, inside the c. 2,200 Ma entry

facts.text: Stromatolites became a major part of the fossil record from about 2,700 Ma; the earliest of confirmed microbial origin is 2.724 Ga.
Stromatolites of the Bulawayo series in Zimbabwe formed the first verified reef community on Earth.
Found throughout the Archean, stromatolites became common late in the eon.

Fossil page: earliest stromatolite of confirmed microbial origin

facts.text: Sturgeon Lake Caldera in northwestern Ontario formed about 2.7 Ga and is one of the world's best-preserved mineralized calderas.
Explosive felsic eruptions and submarine lava domes left nearly 3,000 m of fill inside the caldera.
Its Mattabi pyroclastic flow is considered the third most voluminous eruptive event.

title: Thin atmosphere in the late Archean

facts.text: Fossil raindrop imprints in 2,700 Ma volcanic ash of South Africa's Ventersdorp Supergroup show air less than twice as dense as today's, likely similar or thinner.
Gas bubbles in Archean lava that solidified at sea level about 2,700 Ma point to an air pressure of only 0.23 ± 0.23 bar.
Both results contradict ideas that very high carbon dioxide or nitrogen kept the Archean warm under the faint young Sun.

title: Algoman (Kenoran) orogeny builds the Superior Craton

facts.text: The Algoman, or Kenoran, orogeny built mountains in the late Archean through repeated continental collisions, compression and subduction.
Terranes now in the Canadian Shield collided about 2,700–2,500 Ma, adding land along a belt from South Dakota to Sudbury, Ontario.
The Superior Craton, the largest Archean craton, was stitched together from terranes in a run of orogenies between 2720 and 2680 Ma.
Subduction drove the docking; dates of about 2,700 Ma near Rainy Lake, Ontario, favour a moving-plate model for the boundary.
The orogeny closed the Archean about 2,500 Ma; by then the continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick.

title: Nickel famine in the oceans begins

facts.text: From 2.7 to 2.4 Ga, nickel deposition fell steadily from 400 times today's level.
Methane-making microbes need nickel; as volcanic nickel dwindled, oxygen producers began to outcompete them.
Between about 2.640 and 2.516 Ga, two successive stromatolite-built carbonate platforms grew in the Transvaal Basin on the Kaapvaal craton.
The oldest known giant carbonate platform dates from about 2,600 Ma.
A marine transgression of the Transvaal continental sea flooded tidal flats about 2.550 Ga.

title: Great Dyke intrudes the Zimbabwe Craton

facts.text: A 550 km band of layered ultramafic intrusions, 3–12 km wide, was emplaced across the Zimbabwe Craton about 2.575 Ga.
It has stayed undeformed since intrusion, showing that the craton had already stabilised.
It holds major chromium and platinum resources, one of the world's three most significant platinum sources.
Arctica, a hypothetical continent, formed about 2.565 Ga from the Siberian, Slave, Wyoming, Superior and North Atlantic cratons.
The Algoman, or Kenoran, orogeny assembled it from the Canadian Shield and the Siberian craton.
Rogers argued that it later rifted and reassembled along the 1.8 Ga Trans-Hudson and Taltson-Thelon orogenies.

facts.text: The earliest evidence of microbes oxidizing sulfur, about 2.52 Ga, comes from South Africa's Gamohaan Formation.
It shows sulfur-oxidizing bacteria evolved before the Great Oxidation Event.
Microbial sulfur oxidation is a process in which microorganisms oxidize reduced sulfur compounds to get energy, often supporting carbon fixation by autotrophs.
Only bacteria and archaea oxidize reduced sulfur compounds.

title: Oxygen pulse at the end of the Archean

facts.text: A pulse of higher oxygen around 2,501 Ma is seen by some as a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event.
Studies from 2016–2022 put the onset of atmospheric oxygenation anywhere from 2.7 to 2.3 Ga, including 2.501–2.434 Ga.
Appreciable free oxygen was probably absent from the atmosphere until about 2,500 Ma.

facts.text: Only at the end of the Archean did the continents likely rise above the ocean.
Earlier, much continental crust lay under a superocean deeper than today's, and Paleoarchean crust was still submerged.
By the end of the Archean the continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick under the continents.
Late in the eon, more continental weathering brought ocean oxygen-isotope values down toward modern levels.
